Comments of the
                Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis
    To FERC regarding Mississippi Crossing and South System Expansion 4 projects
                     Docket Nos. CP25-514-000 and CP25-517-000
                                      June 5, 2026


Introduction

The Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) provides the
following comments to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) regarding
the proposed Mississippi Crossing (MSX) and South System Expansion 4 (SSE4) natural
gas pipeline projects, docket numbers CP25-514-000 and CP25-517-000.

In light of recent information, these comments examine the assumptions contained in
the June 2025 ICF Resources (ICF) analyses filed with the Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission (FERC) for Southern Natural Gas Company, LLC and Elba Express
Company, LLC’s South System Expansion 4 methane gas pipeline project (SSE4) and
Tennessee Gas Pipeline Company, LLC’s Mississippi Crossing methane gas pipeline
project (MSX) to evaluate the regional natural gas market need. 1

The comments emphasize that ICF’s conclusions depend on:

      •   A proprietary gas-market model whose material inputs and assumptions are not
          disclosed in a manner that allows independent verification;
      •   Heavy reliance on a highly unlikely High Power energy demand scenario that
          layers aggressive data center and large load assumption onto utility planning
          forecast that already included substantial forecasted data center load growth,
          especially given recent and rapidly changing market dynamics;
      •   A selective framing of historical gas demand peaks that omits relevant longer-
          term context; and
      •   A failure to reconcile regional modeled demand with shipper-specific evidence,
          existing firm transportation, alternative pipeline commitments, and other supply
          and demand-side alternatives.




1
 ICF. Natural Gas Market Analysis – Kinder Morgan, Inc. Mississippi Crossing (MSX) and South System
Expansion 4 (SSE4) Projects, June 10, 2025 (ICF Combined Market Study).


                                                  1
 More recent market dynamics and analyses are discussed in the context of weaknesses
in the ICF analysis that undermine its assessment of both existing and projected
demand. These deficiencies are material, for example, because ICF’s report shows that
the Projects’ most substantial claimed price and reliability benefits occur under the
highly unlikely Hugh Power Case. The reasonableness of that elevated load growth
assumption is thus potentially central to FERC’s market need determination.


Background and overview of ICF modeling approach
MSX is designed to transport up to 2.1 billion cubic feet (bcf) per day of natural gas
capacity over 199 miles of new pipeline extending from Greenville, Mississippi to Butler,
Alabama, plus a seven-mile-long lateral gas pipeline in two counties of Mississippi and
three new natural gas compressor stations.2 The SSE4 project is designed to increase
capacity on the Southern Natural Gas Company’s South Main Line by about 1.3 bcf/day
through construction of roughly 291 miles of non-contiguous natural gas pipeline loops
that would run parallel to the existing South Main Line (22 loops), along with expansions
and modifications to 14 existing compressor stations. 3 The projects—at estimated costs
of $1.7 billion (MSX) and $3.5 billion (SSE4)—are sponsored by Kinder Morgan (with
SSE4 co-sponsored by the Southern Natural Gas Company), and the permitting process
is being expedited under the FAST-41 process coordinated by the Federal Permitting
Improvement Steering Council. 4

Kinder Morgan engaged ICF Resources to conduct an analysis of natural gas and power
markets, and to evaluate the asserted need for new natural gas supplies and pipeline
capacity in Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia and South Carolina, with particular attention to
the SERC Southeastern power markets and related SERC-East demand assumptions. 5
ICF concluded a market need for the MSX and SSE4 projects based primarily on
speculative projections about rapid data center growth in the region and an
oversimplified modeling approach that assumes incremental demand will almost entirely
be met by natural gas rather than in tandem with other supply-side or demand-side
alternatives. 6

                                                   2
 ICF presents energy demand growth forecasts for the SERC-Southeast and SERC-East
reliability assessment areas under both a Base Case and a High Power Case. ICF’s High
Power Case is used to assess how higher growth in the electric sector—heavily driven
by data centers—could increase gas demand and pipeline use, supporting the need for
MSX and SSE4.

To model the market need, ICF uses its proprietary Gas Market Model (GMM), which
inputs demand forecasts (power generators, industry, residential/commercial uses, and
exports) and supply considerations (basin production, pipeline constraints, supply
curves) to identify a balanced level of gas production, prices, pipeline flows and
congestions, and trade flows in future years. 7

The GMM is effectively a black box that restricts review of the inner workings of the
model and many of the key data inputs and assumptions that drive its results. ICF refers
to a “drivers” spreadsheet on which, it states, “The user provides assumptions for
weather, economic growth, oil prices, and gas supply deliverability, among other
variables.” 8 The ICF report does not provide insight or explanation of the validity of key
assumptions, however, including with regard to economic growth, storage and pipeline
expansions, and gas and oil prices.

This lack of transparency is a substantial hindrance to third party review and verification.

Nevertheless, based on the components of ICF’s modeling approach that can be
assessed, it is clear that the simplified gas-market-focused modeling underrepresents
the potential roles of other supply and demand-side alternatives and likely overstates
demand.

ICF’s Base Case demand assumptions, as explained below, actually demonstrate limited
capacity constraints. ICF’s modeling only finds market need for the two pipeline projects
based on its more speculative High Power Case, which assumes aggressive expansion
of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers in the region.

ICF’s Base Case analysis also demonstrates that the projects’ claimed consumer price
benefits are minimal absent the High Power Assumptions. For the Base Case, the study
projects only a $0.01 per million metric Btu (MMBtu) average delivered-price reduction
from 2029 to 2045, with winter discounts reaching up to $0.10/MMBtu. The larger
claimed benefits depend on the High Power Case.

                                                   3
         I.      ICF’s conclusion that gas demand is historically
                trending upward is based on incomplete data and
                misguided emphasis
ICF’s baseline assessment of historical natural gas demand in Mississippi, Alabama,
Georgia, and South Carolina draws a conclusion based on incomplete data.

Consolidating residential, commercial, industrial and power demand across the four
states, ICF concludes, “The rising frequency and magnitude of peak demands signal a
pressing need for infrastructure enhancements to maintain reliability and ensure
sufficient supply.” 9 Using an illustration of daily gas demand from 2019 through early
2025 (see Figure 1 below), ICF points to a higher peak day in 2025 (9.1 bcf on January
21, 2025) compared with 2024 (8.6 bcf on January 20, 2024).

Figure 1: ICF Combined Market Study Fig. 16: Daily Historical Natural Gas
Deliveries in the Residential, Commercial, Industrial and Power Sectors in
Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, and South Carolina from 2019 through 2025 10




But it is not clear why ICF presented data that went back only six years, choosing to
start in 2019 (see Figure 1). Figure 2 shows that just one year earlier, in 2018, the
highest peak demand of the past decade was set on January 17th at 9.4 bcf. Also, adding
current data from 2026 shows the peak demand that occurred on January 31 of this
year was back down to 8.6 bcf, as occurred in 2024 (Figure 2). 11




9
  ICF Combined Market Study, p. 10.
10
   ICF Combined Market Study, Figure 16, p. 39. Historical natural gas deliveries are sourced from
interstate pipeline informational postings and Hitachi Energy.
11
   Hitachi Energy Velocity Suite. Natural Gas Demand by Customer Type.

                                                    4
 Figure 2: Expanded Version of ICF Fig. 16: Daily Natural Gas Demand by Customer
Type and Annual Average Daily Demand in Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, and
South Carolina from 2017 through early 2026 12




The broader picture does not illustrate a consistent increasing trend. Instead, as the
expanded Figure 2 illustrates, demand levels have demonstrated relative stability over
the past decade with isolated peaks driven by specific weather events. The peak
demand on January 21, 2025 was driven by a historic winter storm in the southern U.S.
that saw locations in all these states set records for snowfall and cold temperatures. 13
The high demand that occurred on January 17, 2018, was due to Winter Storm Inga. 14
Figure 2 illustrates that the annual average daily demand has remained fairly constant
over the past decade, and actually has had an annual average decline in demand of
0.78% between 2017 and 2025, while the peak demand spikes are variable rather than
trending upward.

The historical gas demand in the region does not illustrate a rapid change or “pressing
need,” but rather a period of general stability with idiosyncratic peaks driven by
individual severe weather events. Although regions need to plan for the likelihood of
sporadic weather events, constructing a large pipeline (or two) for a need that occurs on
only occasional days is very likely not the most cost-effective approach to energy
management.

        II.     ICF’s High Power Case substantially—and likely
               unreasonably—exceeds the forecasts by the North
               American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC)

Without a granular shipper-level review (as discussed in Section IV below), ICF’s
market need determination resorts to proprietary forecasting assumptions and depends
on a highly questionable “High Power” forecast driven by an assertion that electricity
demand growth will accelerate in the region. These regional demand assumptions play a
key role in supporting ICF’s broader conclusions that additional gas-fired generation and
associated pipeline capacity will be needed in the Southeast. Before discussing the
specific utility IRPs and planning documents ICF relies on to build up its electricity
demand forecasts, this section compares ICF’s regional forecast in its High Power Case
with the regional forecasts produced by NERC—the FERC-certified authority whose
mission is to assure the effective, efficient reduction of risks to electric grid reliability and
security.
ICF presents electricity demand growth forecasts for the SERC-Southeast and SERC-
East reliability assessment areas under both its Base Case and High Power cases. As
discussed, ICF’s High Power Case is used to assess how higher electric-sector growth,
driven by data centers, could increase natural gas demand and pipeline utilization,
therefore supporting the need for MSX and SSE4.
ICF’s High Power Case is a load-growth sensitivity layered onto its Base Case forecast.
For SERC-Southeast and SERC-East, ICF starts with utility planning sources, including
IRPs, utilities’ reports to FERC (Form 714), and utility-specific planning updates, then
adds incremental large-load assumptions tied to data centers, industrial growth, and
economic-development activity. In SERC-Southeast, ICF’s High Power Case adds 10.5
GW of large load by 2033 and 12.4 GW by 2040 relative to the Base Case. In SERC-
East, it adds 2.6 GW by 2033 and 4.0 GW by 2040. 15
These assumptions can be compared against demand forecasts published by NERC, the
FERC-certified electric reliability organization.
NERC’s Electricity Supply & Demand database provides annually published 10-year
projections for the North American bulk power system. These forecasts are submitted
by NERC Regions on an assessment-area basis and are reviewed through NERC’s Long
Term Reliability Assessment (LTRA) process. 16 For large loads, NERC’s 2025 LTRA
states that demand and large-load projections are based on load-serving entity and bulk
power system planner forecasts provided to NERC during LTRA development, reflecting

      2026   49,517      48,386       2.3%         45,861      44,414     3.2%

By 2035, ICF’s summer peak forecast is approximately 12% higher than NERC in the
SERC-Southeast region and 14% higher in SERC-East, demonstrating that ICF’s High
Power Case is significantly in excess compared to NERC’s widely used regional
reliability benchmark, which already incorporates large-load expectations.

Because ICF’s most expansive claims regarding pipeline constraints, reliability risks, and
price benefits occur under the High Power Case, the question of the reasonableness of
its elevated load growth assumption is central to evaluating the credibility of its market
need conclusions.

                                               7
           III.    Despite AI’s financial issues and public concern
                  about energy affordability, ICF bases its demand
                  forecasts on speculative assumptions about data
                  center growth—amplified by overestimated utility
                  forecasts
NERC observes that, “New data centers for artificial intelligence and the digital economy
account for most of the projected increase in North American electricity demand over
the next 10 years.”19 In this context, NERC cautioned in its 2025 LTRA that:

             “ERCOT and PJM, the grid planners and operators for two areas
             experiencing vigorous large-load and data center development, have
             each prepared revised load forecasts since the 2025 LTRA data
             collection period that, due to timing, is not used in this LTRA. Both
             forecasts indicate that some large-load projects have slowed or failed to
             materialize within the shorter-term horizon, while interconnection
             requests for later years continue to increase. Load forecasts that are
             revised downward can shrink the energy shortfalls that are projected in
             this LTRA.” 20

But, as explained below, even the interconnection requests for later years may not
materialize as expected, due to weaknesses in the AI business model.

      A. Data centers are becoming high-profile affordability
         issues for electricity and natural gas service ratepayers,
         and stability risks require close management.
Ratepayers are subsidizing the cost of infrastructure being built to serve data centers,
and this subsidization will worsen if infrastructure is overbuilt. Typically, utilities treat
data centers like any other large commercial or industrial customer, and the cost to
build infrastructure needed to serve them (including natural gas pipelines) is rolled into
the receiving utility’s overall rate base. But some utilities today are building
infrastructure that simply would not be needed at all, or not needed at the large scale
proposed, if not for data centers—and the rate structure has all customers paying for it.

IEEFA identified a clear example of this phenomenon in Virginia. Dominion Virginia
Power disclosed that it classifies some of the transmission infrastructure projects it plans

 to construct through 2031 as “data center driven projects,” whose need is driven solely
by data centers. The $2.4 billion price tag Dominion estimated for such projects will be
paid by utility ratepayers across the PJM customer base.21 The Virginia Joint Legislative
Audit and Review Committee concluded that as a result of growing data center load:

           “A typical residential customer of Dominion Energy could experience
           generation- and transmission-related costs increasing by an estimated
           $14 to $37 monthly in constant (or real) dollars by 2040 (independent of
           inflation).” 22

As data center loads have grown rapidly over the last few years, creating new
challenges for utilities and regulators, several jurisdictions have established large load
tariffs (predominantly aimed at data center customers) designed to ensure that data
centers pay their fair share of costs. Examples of approved tariffs can be found in
Virginia, 23 Ohio,24 Michigan, 25 Wisconsin,26 West Virginia, 27 and elsewhere. The design of
specific tariff provisions (contract length, minimum charges, termination payments,
collateral requirements, etc.) determines how protective any given tariff actually is of
existing ratepayers.

There are no ratepayer protections in place in the Southeast, however, that would
prevent ratepayers from shouldering the costs of building the MSX and SSE4 pipelines,

 which will be baked into the natural gas prices charged to the pipelines’ contractors for

IEEFA is further concerned that if and when the AI bubble bursts, it will likely lead to
bankruptcies, a cooling off of investment in the sector, and very likely fewer operational
data centers than currently forecasted. This poses a financial risk for electricity and
natural gas ratepayers, who may be left paying for the costs of unused or underused
infrastructure capacity. Ultimately, the ratepayers may have to shoulder the costs of the
pipelines as well as stranded electrical transmission and generation assets that are not
written off. Also, to the extent that electric utilities have entered into firm transportation
agreements for natural gas pipeline capacity that they are unable to re-sell, ratepayers
will also be on the hook for these costs.

An additional issue arises for electricity consumers when data center operations present
unexpected surges or drops in demand that affect grid operations. NERC issued a rare
Level 3 alert on May 4th of this year, raising concerns about the readiness of utilities to
manage incidents of rapidly oscillating demand. NERC posted seven strong
recommendations, termed “Essential Actions,” that NERC-registered entities should
consider. 29 The stated purpose of the alert is, “to ensure Essential Actions are taken by
registered entities to address the risks posed by existing and new computational loads
interacting with the bulk power system (BBP).” 30 Among other measures, the Level 3
alert urges utilities and grid managers to establish a commissioning process for
computational loads with testing requirements, and also to revise definitions that trigger
a review of local area protections, stability limits and other reliability studies to account
for computational loads. 31

Public concerns about electricity costs, grid stability impacts, water usage and other
issues may affect the trajectory of data center development and the amount of new data
center demand that develops.

      B. Fundamental weakness in the AI data center business
        model calls into question long-term forecasts of data
        center demand.
Long-term forecasts of data center demand may not materialize to the extent projected,
due to fundamental weaknesses in the business model.

Certain flagship AI operations remain deeply unprofitable, with an uncertain path to
profitability. 32 The Wall Street Journal this spring noted concerns about OpenAI having
missed its own targets for new users and revenue, while engaging in massive data-
center spending in the face of slowing growth.33 In an opinion piece, Henry Blodget,
former editor of the Business Insider, discussed OpenAI’s situation in the historical
context of the dot.com bubble, stating:

           “So the question for the OpenAI community—and the much broader
           community fueling and feasting on the AI market bubble—is whether
           Open AI’s problems are limited to OpenAI…or a sign that this first jaw-
           dropping era of AI euphoria and growth is coming to an end.”34

Profitability concerns extent to Anthropic as well. 35 In general, competition among AI
models is holding subscription prices below levels that cover the actual costs of building

Profitability is also challenged by growing—and potentially still understated—expenses
related to depreciation. AI companies incur high depreciation costs because the chips
used in data centers have a short useful life. 37 Depreciation charges, notes The Wall
Street Journal, “are eating into earnings at Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon.”38

Also, on a practical level, experts have raised concern that not enough chips are being
produced globally to meet purported U.S. data center demand. London Economics
International LLC (LEI), on behalf of the Southern Environmental Law Center, conducted
an analysis of the question in 2025 and found the projected number of U.S. data centers
would require roughly 90% of globally produced semiconductor chips through 2030. 39
Such an outcome would be unrealistic given that the U.S. currently accounts for less
than half of global data center installed capacity and faces competition for chips from
Europe, Canada, China and parts of Asia and the Middle East.40

The problem persists today, and the market consequences are widespread. Vidya Mani,
a global supply chains expert and associate professor of business administration at the
University of Virginia, recently published a briefing on how AI is reorganizing the chip
market. Mani cautions that only a small number of producers both design and
manufacture memory chips, and the process is “extraordinarily capital-intensive.” 41
Mani explains that the memory chip industry has experienced repeated cycles of
overcapacity and undersupply—from the post-dot-com collapse and 2007-2009 glut
through the 2022-23 downturn and the AI-driven tight market of 2024 and 2025—
heightening the risk of having costly fabrication plants (fabs) go underused. The industry
has responded with consolidation and greater focus on higher-margin products rather

     C. ICF’s electricity demand forecasts rely on speculative
        data center growth assumptions layered onto utility
        forecasting that also includes data center forecasts.

ICF’s High Power Case is a load-growth sensitivity layered onto its Base Case forecast.
For SERC-Southeast and SERC-East, ICF starts with utility planning sources, including
integrated resource plans (IRPs), utilities’ reports to FERC (Form 714), and utility-
specific planning updates. It then adds incremental large-load assumptions tied to data
centers, industrial growth and economic development activity. 50

But ICF’s reliance on utility planning materials in establishing its Base Case incorporates
large load assumptions made at the utility level, particularly related to data center
electricity demand growth, that are highly speculative. These may include early-stage
project inquiries as well as development projects that may not ultimately become
executed contracts or operational load.

       IV.     ICF’s demand forecasting fails to analyze whether
               shipper precedent agreements overstate demand
ICF states that its short-term projections for residential and commercial gas demand rely
on local distribution company (LDC) portfolio plans, but its longer-term projections are
based on historical relationships among gas consumption, population growth and
economic growth. 73 ICF’s long-term model is inadequate because it cannot serve as a
substitute for the actual demand forecasts and resource plans of the specific utilities that
have contracted for capacity on MSX and SSE4.

ICF’s framework over-simplifies the way individual LDCs and electric utilities plan for gas
needs. It aggregates demand across broad sectors and geographies, relying on
modeled relationships and regional assumptions, rather than testing whether each
anchor shipper’s own publicly disclosed load forecasts, supply resources, existing firm
transportation (FT) contracts (as opposed to service that can be interrupted in times of
heavy demand), and alternative pipeline commitments support the specific volume of
capacity for which the shipper subscribed through precedent agreements.

Environmental Law Center, assessed each shipper’s projected demand for natural gas,
including for gas-fired generation or LDCs. LEI compared that demand to the shippers’
own publicly available resource plans, design-day supply plans, existing FT contracts
and other pipeline expansion commitments.74 LEI states:

       V.      ICF does not analyze existing use of regional
               pipelines or the potential impact of planned pipeline
               expansions
ICF argues that the current pipelines serving the region—Tennessee Gas Pipeline
(TGP), Midcontinent Express Pipeline (ME), Southern Natural Gas (SNG), and
Transcontinental Pipeline (Transco)—are likely to become constrained because (i)
certain segments of TGP had utilization above 90% across 18% of days between 2019
and 2024; (ii) one segment of MEP had utilization above 90% across 73% of days
between 2019 and 2024 (although peak utilization actually occurred in 2022 and has
subsided in more recent years), and (iii) marginal increases in end-use deliveries by
SNG occurred during certain peak periods. 82 ICF does not, however, present a system-
wide analysis of whether historical pipeline use trends across all southeast regional
pipelines demonstrate a consistent and growing capacity constraint for the region.
Instead, ICF selectively identifies pipeline segments that have been heavily used during
certain periods.

(Southeast Energy connector, Alabama to Georgia Connector, and Southeast Supply
Enhancement Project). Its report asserts the Transco expansions are fully subscribed
and “are insufficient to meet projected demand growth expectations.” 83 But ICF fails to

Conclusion
For the reasons stated above, ICF’s market analysis of the MSX and SSE4 pipeline
projects is incomplete and inadequate. FERC should revisit the analysis, as the issues
raised in these comments go to the heart of the question of whether the two pipeline
projects meet the requirements for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity,
which would be required to construct and operate the pipelines.
